[DOCUMENTED SUMMARY, paraphrased from public sources] The U.S. EEOC alleged that a tutoring company programmed its application software to automatically reject older applicants (women aged 55 or older and men aged 60 or older), rejecting more than 200 qualified U.S. applicants (count stored as a lower bound). The company denied wrongdoing and the case was settled by a 2023 consent decree providing $365,000 to affected applicants. The allegations were not adjudicated. Rejections are reported for March and April 2020 (exact dates not given).
Source_Reference: EEOC press releases: 'EEOC Sues iTutorGroup for Age Discrimination' (5 May 2022) and 'iTutorGroup to Pay $365,000 to Settle EEOC Discriminatory Hiring Suit' (11 Sep 2023): https://eeoc.gov/newsroom/itutorgroup-pay-365000-settle-eeoc-discriminatory-hiring-suit

Incident_Description: [DOCUMENTED SUMMARY, paraphrased from public sources] OpenAI reported that a bug in an open-source library caused some users to see titles from other users' chat histories, and that payment-related information (name, email, payment address, card type, last four digits and expiry date) of about 1.2% of ChatGPT Plus subscribers active in a nine-hour window may have been visible to others. OpenAI said the number of users whose data was actually revealed was extremely low and notified affected users. The total number of people is not stated in the source.
Source_Reference: OpenAI, 'March 20 ChatGPT outage: Here's what happened' (24 Mar 2023): https://openai.com/blog/march-20-chatgpt-outage

AI_System: Facial recognition system used for a Detroit police investigation
Incident_Description: [DOCUMENTED SUMMARY, paraphrased from public sources] Reports state that a man in Detroit was arrested in January 2020 after a facial recognition match wrongly identified him as a shoplifting suspect, was held for about 30 hours, and that the charges were later dismissed. Detroit police said they do not arrest on facial recognition alone. Remedy outcomes are not recorded here.
Source_Reference: NPR, 'The Computer Got It Wrong' (24 Jun 2020): https://www.npr.org/2020/06/24/882683463/the-computer-got-it-wrong-how-facial-recognition-led-to-a-false-arrest-in-mich ; ACLU First Amended Complaint: https://assets.aclu.org/live/uploads/2024/01/54.-First-Amended-Complaint.pdf

AI_System: Dutch tax authority risk-classification model (childcare benefits)
Incident_Description: [DOCUMENTED SUMMARY, paraphrased from public sources] Amnesty International reported that the Dutch tax authorities used a risk-classification algorithm introduced in 2013 in which nationality was a risk factor, giving non-Dutch nationals higher risk scores. Tens of thousands of parents and caregivers, mostly from low-income families, were falsely accused of fraud, and the scandal brought down the Dutch government in January 2021. Amnesty also reported that civil servants were given no information on why a high-risk score was produced, and an absence of accountability.

[DOCUMENTED SUMMARY, paraphrased from public sources] The Royal Commission into Australia's Robodebt scheme reported that an automated debt-raising process based on averaging income data from tax records generated debts, many not owed; income averaging used this way was reported as inconsistent with social security legislation, and the Federal Court had found the method unlawful in 2019. Reports describe roughly half a million debts or nearly half a million people (figures differ), so the number of people is stored as unknown. A class action was settled in 2020.
Source_Reference: Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme, Final Report (7 Jul 2023); coverage: https://www.jurist.org/news/2023/07/australia-robodebt-royal-commission-hands-down-findings-recommends-referrals-for-prosecution ; https://www.sbs.com.au/news/article/robodebt-report-recommends-welfare-payment-increase-in-lieu-of-compensation/fvhxwtutj

AI_System: Commercial health-risk prediction algorithm studied by Obermeyer et al.
Incident_Description: [DOCUMENTED SUMMARY, paraphrased from public sources] A peer-reviewed study reported racial bias in a widely used commercial algorithm that predicts patients' health-care needs: patients identified as Black were assigned lower risk scores than equally sick White patients, because the algorithm used health-care costs as a proxy for need. The number of affected people is not stored here.
Source_Reference: Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, Mullainathan S. 'Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations.' Science 366(6464):447-453 (25 Oct 2019). URL not captured in this build; verify against the original before publication.

Incident_Description: [DOCUMENTED SUMMARY, paraphrased from public sources] Reuters reported that Amazon built an experimental machine-learning recruiting tool that learned to downgrade resumes containing terms associated with women, and that the project was abandoned. Amazon is reported to have said the tool was not used to evaluate candidates, so the real-world effect on applicants is not established.
Source_Reference: Reuters (J. Dastin), 'Amazon scraps secret AI recruiting tool that showed bias against women' (10 Oct 2018). URL not captured in this build; verify against the original before publication.

Incident_Description: [DOCUMENTED SUMMARY, paraphrased from public sources] In November 2019, public allegations said Apple Card credit-limit decisions gave women lower limits than men with comparable finances. The New York State Department of Financial Services investigated and, in a report published in March 2021, reported finding no violation of fair-lending law. Exact dates and the number of people are not stored.
Source_Reference: New York State Department of Financial Services, report on its Apple Card investigation (March 2021); public allegations began November 2019. URL not captured in this build; verify against the original before publication.

Incident_Description: [DOCUMENTED SUMMARY, paraphrased from public sources] A job applicant sued Workday alleging that its AI-based applicant-screening tools discriminated on the basis of race, age and disability. The claims are allegations, are contested, and the current case status should be re-checked.
Source_Reference: Mobley v. Workday, Inc., U.S. District Court, Northern District of California, No. 3:23-cv-00770 (filed 2023). URL not captured in this build; verify against the original before publication. Re-check case status.

Incident_Description: [DOCUMENTED SUMMARY, paraphrased from public sources] The UK Information Commissioner's Office fined Clearview AI about 7.5 million pounds in May 2022 for collecting images of people from the web and social media to build a facial-recognition database without their knowledge, finding breaches of UK data protection law. The number of affected people and the exact date are not stored.
Source_Reference: UK Information Commissioner's Office, monetary penalty and announcement concerning Clearview AI Inc. (May 2022). URL not captured in this build; verify against the original before publication.

Incident_Description: [DOCUMENTED SUMMARY, paraphrased from public sources] ProPublica analysed risk scores produced by the COMPAS tool for defendants in Broward County, Florida, and reported racial disparities in its errors (Black defendants more often wrongly labelled higher risk). The tool's developer disputed the analysis. The number of people affected is not stored.
Source_Reference: ProPublica (Angwin, Larson, Mattu, Kirchner), 'Machine Bias' (23 May 2016). URL not captured in this build; verify against the original before publication.

Incident_Description: [DOCUMENTED SUMMARY, paraphrased from public sources] An Italian court in Bologna ruled that the algorithm Deliveroo used to rank riders and allocate shifts was discriminatory because it penalised cancellations or absences without distinguishing legitimate reasons such as illness. The number of riders affected is not stored; Report_Date is the ruling date.
Source_Reference: Tribunale di Bologna, ordinanza of 31 Dec 2020 (Filcams CGIL, Nidil CGIL, Filt CGIL v Deliveroo Italia S.r.l.), as reported by the press. URL not captured in this build; verify against the original before publication.

Incident_Description: [DOCUMENTED SUMMARY, paraphrased from public sources] In August 2020, exam results in England were adjusted by a statistical standardisation model. After widespread criticism that many students' grades had been lowered, the UK government announced it would use teacher-assessed grades instead. Whether the model counts as AI is not established (hence AI_Attribution SUSPECTED); the number of students is not stored.
Source_Reference: UK Government and Ofqual announcements of 17 Aug 2020 reverting to teacher-assessed grades; widely reported. URL not captured in this build; verify against the original before publication.

Incident_Description: [DOCUMENTED SUMMARY, paraphrased from public sources] A tribunal in British Columbia found Air Canada responsible for incorrect information about bereavement fares given to a customer by its website chatbot, rejecting the airline's argument that the chatbot was a separate entity. The money amount is not stored because it was awarded in Canadian dollars and this dataset uses USD only.
Source_Reference: Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149 (British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal, February 2024). URL not captured in this build; verify against the original before publication.

Incident_Description: [DOCUMENTED SUMMARY, paraphrased from public sources] Michigan's automated unemployment-insurance system (MiDAS), used from about 2013, automatically flagged claimants for fraud with little human review; the state later acknowledged that many determinations were wrong. Counts and exact dates are not stored.
Source_Reference: Reporting by the Detroit Free Press and other outlets (2015 to 2017) and Michigan Unemployment Insurance Agency statements. URL not captured in this build; verify against the original before publication.
